Security & Custody

Patches at the Perimeter: Wallet Makers Harden as Attacks Move Up the Stack

A flurry of security releases from Bisq, Sparrow, and Specter DIY underscores a year where infrastructure is under continuous fire—and custody is where the fault lines run.

The releases arrived in quick succession over twenty-four hours, each carrying the same underlying urgency: the software and hardware guarding private keys is under active, deliberate siege across the ecosystem. Bisq announced version 1.10.8, a mandatory update addressing vulnerabilities surfaced during an external security audit. As the project stated plainly: Bisq v1.10.8 is released. This important security update fixes vulnerabilities identified during our recent security audit. Updating to this version is required to continue trading. (source)

On the desktop side, Craig Raw released Sparrow Wallet 2.5.5, incorporating bug fixes and security reviews (source), while Specter DIY tagged v1.10.5, reinforcing hardware randomness and output verification routines (source).

The relentless cadence of disclosures reflects a structural shift in adversary economics. In a widely circulated analysis, Ungovernable laid out the reality confronting developers and users alike:

The reason it feels like every week now is that it is every week now.

If you run a software project or a hardware project or anything that handles Bitcoin, people are attacking your shit right now. Not eventually. Right now.

Think about it from their side. Steal personal information and you still have to find a buyer. Steal from the software that holds the money and you are done.

Ungovernable (source)

Yet the week's most alarming compromises did not breach cryptographic primitives; they bypassed device firmware entirely by targeting the mundane communications pipes of third-party SaaS vendors. Freedom.Tech documented the ongoing fallout of the recent Brevo incident, where attackers breached marketing accounts belonging to Trezor, BitBox, and CoinTracking:

On 9 September, customers of Trezor, BitBox and CoinTracking received emails warning of an STM32 entropy vulnerability and asking them to take action on their hardware wallet.

The emails came from those companies' real domains. SPF passed. DKIM passed. Every check your mail provider runs to prove a message came from where it claims to have come from, passed, because it genuinely had.

Attackers had access to Brevo, the email marketing platform those companies send through, and created API keys inside their accounts.

The weak point was never the wallet maker. It was the vendor they trusted to send their post.

Freedom.Tech (source)

The lesson applies equally to custodial finance. Following reports that digital bank Revolut surrendered unencrypted identification documents, selfies, and complete transaction histories in response to a forged subpoena without requiring an actual breach, Dee Kay articulated the only enduring defense:

The only way not to leak private and sensitive customer data is not having it in the first place.... (source)

Dispatches & Infrastructure

Operating Systems

GrapheneOS Details Google's Private Android 17 APIs

GrapheneOS (source)

The GrapheneOS team published an architectural breakdown documenting that Google's Android 17 QPR1 release introduces developer APIs exclusive to Pixel hardware without providing the code to AOSP:

Android 17 QPR1 is the first release since Android Honeycomb (3.x) adding new APIs for app developers without a release to the Android Open Source Project. The new APIs are currently exclusive to the Pixel OS and aren't available to other Android OEMs.

The report highlighted escalating friction between upstream Android and independent distributions, noting that security patches to standard platform components are also being staggered:

Google should not be gatekeeping security patches to the standard Android platform code from Android OEMs but that's what they've started doing.

On hardware protection, the team confirmed Memory Tagging Extensions (MTE) are preserved in Pixel 11 silicon despite being disabled in shipping firmware: Pixel 11 didn't remove it from hardware, only firmware, so that's good news.

The Wire

NWC Wallet Interoperability & Blossom Handling

Ecosystem Round

Testing client compliance across Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC), Dee Kay ran multi-wallet audits through BrollyZapper and Amethyst (source). Findings revealed divergent interpretations of budget authorizations and payment hash receipts between custodial lightning providers and Cashu ecash mints.

In parallel, Vitor Pamplona updated Amethyst's media transport layer to resolve Blossom upload failures where servers refuse JSON manifests under issue 113 (source).

The subjective experience of protocol drift was observed by M✨️, noting how differing subscription filters between Amethyst, Wisp, and Primal fragment timelines into distinct conversations (source).

Releases

New Releases: Tenna, Armada, and BuhoGO

Client Desks

Tooling and client releases continued across mobile and desktop environments:

Tenna entered public TestFlight with native iOS audio streaming built on Nostr protocols, supporting background playback and inline zap receipts.

Armada published its updated local-mesh synchronization engine, allowing offline nodes to exchange signed events directly over Bluetooth Low Energy and local subnets before gossiping to relays.

BuhoGO released version 1.9.2, refining Cashu mint balance consolidation and introducing automated seed phrase export verification for mobile ecash wallets.
